Rao-Scott chi-square test for a survey table

Source: R/rscchi.R
rscchi.Rd

The test of independence of two categorical variables in a two-way table from a stratified, clustered and weighted sample (a victimisation or justice survey, say), with Rao and Scott's corrections for the design, to go with the estimates of svymx() and the tables of ctabx(). Pearson's statistic on such data is too large: the design makes the cell proportions vary more than simple random sampling, and the corrections divide it by the design effects.

Usage

rscchi(x, y, w = NULL, strata = NULL, psu = NULL, fpc = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'rscchi'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x, y

The two variables: labels (numbers, text or a factor), one per respondent, each with two labels or more; for print(), x is an object of class rscchi.

w

NULL or the sampling weights: positive numbers.

strata

NULL or the stratum of each respondent: labels.

psu

NULL (each respondent its own) or the first-stage unit of each respondent: labels.

fpc

NULL or the number of first-stage units in the population of each respondent's stratum (constant within strata).

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class rscchi, a list: tab, the weighted cell proportions (a matrix, x by y); test, a data frame (test: pearson, rs1, rs2, f; stat, df1, df2, p); deff, the generalised design effects; dbar and a2, their mean and squared coefficient of variation; and des (n, strata, psu, df).

Details

The cell proportions p are weighted; Pearson's X^2 is computed on them scaled to the number of respondents n, X^2 = n sum (p_ij - p_i. p_.j)^2 / (p_i. p_.j). Their covariance V comes by linearisation over the first-stage units within strata, as svymx() reads the design (Lumley 2004). The generalised design effects deff are the eigenvalues of Delta = (C' D^-1 C / n)^-1 (C' D^-1 V D^-1 C), C a basis of the interaction contrasts and D the diagonal of p (Rao and Scott 1984). The tests: pearson, X^2 on K = (r - 1)(c - 1) degrees of freedom, wrong under the design; rs1, the first-order correction X^2 / mean(deff) on K; rs2, the second-order (Satterthwaite) correction X^2 / (mean(deff) (1 + a^2)) on K / (1 + a^2), a the coefficient of variation of the design effects; and f, X^2 / sum(deff) as an F on d0 = K / (1 + a^2) and d0 nu degrees of freedom, nu the first-stage units less the strata, the form Thomas and Rao (1987) found to hold its level best. They agree with survey::svychisq() ("Chisq" for rs1, "F" for f).

References

Rao, J. N. K. and Scott, A. J. (1981). The analysis of categorical data from complex sample surveys: chi-squared tests for goodness of fit and independence in two-way tables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 76(374), 221-230. doi:10.1080/01621459.1981.10477633

Rao, J. N. K. and Scott, A. J. (1984). On chi-squared tests for multiway contingency tables with cell proportions estimated from survey data. The Annals of Statistics, 12(1), 46-60. doi:10.1214/aos/1176346391

Thomas, D. R. and Rao, J. N. K. (1987). Small-sample comparisons of level and power for simple goodness-of-fit statistics under cluster sampling. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 630-636. doi:10.1080/01621459.1987.10478476

Lumley, T. (2004). Analysis of complex survey samples. Journal of Statistical Software, 9(8), 1-19. doi:10.18637/jss.v009.i08

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(region = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 60),
                block = rep(1:12, each = 10),
                age = sample(c("young", "middle", "old"), 120, TRUE),
                w = runif(120, 50, 150))
d$victim <- rbinom(120, 1, ifelse(d$age == "young", 0.35, 0.2))
rscchi(d$age, d$victim, d$w, d$region, d$block)
#> rscchi: 3 x 2 table, 120 respondents, 2 strata, 12 first-stage units
#>     test  stat   df1   df2       p
#>  pearson 5.539 2.000    NA 0.06271
#>      rs1 3.254 2.000    NA 0.19650
#>      rs2 3.134 1.926    NA 0.19750
#>        f 1.627 1.926 19.26 0.22264
